items.prompt: What does 'concurrency' mean, as this unit defines it?
choices: Multiple tasks making progress over the same period of time, without necessarily executing at the exact same instant
Multiple tasks always executing at the literal same instant, which requires multiple CPU cores
A single task running as fast as the hardware possibly allows it to go
A guarantee built into the runtime that no task will ever have to wait for another
items.explanation: Concurrency only requires that tasks take turns and interleave — it doesn't require literal simultaneous execution, which is what parallelism specifically means.
items.reference:
Concurrency vs. parallelism
concurrency: progress over the same period
parallelism: same literal instant, needs multiple threads/cores

Why: concurrency doesn't require parallelism, though the two are often used loosely as synonyms.
items.reflection: Concurrency vs. parallelism shows up outside computing too: a single cashier switching between two customers' orders is concurrency without parallelism; two cashiers serving two customers at once is parallelism. Where else have you seen “taking turns” versus “genuinely simultaneous” show up — a shared kitchen, one therapist juggling clients, a single parking attendant?
